stem.text: Stomata in leaves respond to changes in environmental conditions by opening and closing. This regulates carbon dioxide uptake and water loss.
Describe the mechanism by which stomata open in sunlight.

points.text: protons / H+ ions, pumped, from guard cells / into guard cell wall ;
ref. to negative potential (inside cell) or Cl– ions enter (cell) ;
(voltage-gated) K+ channels open or K+ ions enter (guard) cells ;
water enters cell, by osmosis / down water potential gradient ;
(guard) cells, become turgid / swell / increase in volume ;

markScheme.note: MS instruction says any four, but five points are listed (as on the printed MS).

explanation.text: Opening stomata in light starts with active pumping of H+ out of the guard cell. This makes the inside of the cell more negative, which drives Cl- in and opens voltage-gated K+ channels so K+ also enters. The rising solute concentration inside the guard cell lowers its water potential, so water follows by osmosis, making the guard cell turgid and changing its shape so the pore opens.

reasoningChain: H+ is actively pumped out of the guard cell, creating a negative potential inside.
This negative potential draws in Cl- and opens voltage-gated K+ channels, letting K+ in too.
Solute concentration rises inside the cell, lowering its water potential.
Water enters by osmosis down the water potential gradient, the cell becomes turgid, and the stoma opens.

inferredMistakes.text: Starting the explanation at water entering the cell without first explaining why solute concentration rises (the H+ pumping and ion movements that create the osmotic gradient).

stem.text: Stomatal conductance is a measure of the rate of water vapour loss from the intercellular air spaces of leaves to the atmosphere through the stomata.
A student investigated the effect of different concentrations of abscisic acid (ABA) on stomatal conductance in Helianthus annuus, the common sunflower.
The student treated the roots of 15 sunflower plants with different concentrations of ABA solution. The plants were left in standardised conditions for 24 hours.

items: the concentration of ABA in the xylem sap of each plant
the stomatal conductance of the leaves of each plant.

stem.text: The results are shown in Fig. 3.1.

stem.caption: Fig. 3.1
stem.alt: Scatter graph of stomatal conductance in mol per square metre per second against concentration of ABA in the xylem sap in micromol per cubic metre, with a curve of best fit falling steeply from about 2.2 at a low ABA concentration to about 0.2 and levelling off at higher ABA concentrations up to 1000.

stem.text: With reference to Fig. 3.1, describe the relationship between the concentration of ABA in the xylem sap and stomatal conductance.

points.text: as abscisic acid concentration increases stomatal conductance decreases or negative correlation / inverse correlation / inversely proportional ;
two sets of x y figures to support mp 1 with units (at least once) ;
steep decrease in conductance to 100–150 ABA ;
no / little, effect on conductance above 250–425 ABA ;

explanation.text: The curve falls steeply at first and then flattens: there is a negative (inverse) relationship between ABA concentration and stomatal conductance. Quoting actual coordinate pairs from the graph, with units, earns a separate mark from describing the relationship in words.

reasoningChain: State the overall direction: as ABA increases, conductance decreases (negative correlation).
Quote a pair of x/y values from the graph, with units, to support that statement.
Describe the shape in two parts: a steep decrease up to roughly 100-150 of ABA concentration, then little further change above about 250-425.

inferredMistakes.text: Describing only the direction of the relationship without quoting supporting figures from the graph or describing the two-part shape (steep fall, then plateau).

stem.text: Suggest explanations for the results shown in Fig. 3.1.

points.text: ABA binds to receptor on guard cell ;
Ca2+ ions, enter (guard) cells / act as 2nd messenger ;
water leaves so cells become, flaccid / less turgid ;

explanation.text: ABA signals the guard cell to close the stoma, the reverse of the opening mechanism in (a). ABA binds to a receptor on the guard cell, this acts through Ca2+ as a second messenger inside the cell, K+ then leaves the guard cell instead of entering, so water follows by osmosis and leaves too, and the cell becomes flaccid rather than turgid, closing the stoma and lowering stomatal conductance.

reasoningChain: ABA binds to a receptor on the guard cell plasma membrane.
Ca2+ enters the guard cell and acts as a second messenger.
K+ ions leave the guard cell rather than entering as they do in (a).
Water follows by osmosis and leaves the cell, which becomes flaccid, closing the stoma and reducing stomatal conductance.

inferredMistakes.text: Describing the stomata-opening mechanism (H+ pumped out, K+ and Cl- entering) instead of the closing mechanism that ABA triggers.

stem.text: Some transcription factors increase the rate of transcription of genes involved in the closure of stomata.
State where transcription factors bind to cause an increase in the rate of transcription.

explanation.text: Transcription factors that increase transcription rate are activators: they bind to the promoter region of a gene (or to nearby regulatory DNA that influences the promoter), helping RNA polymerase bind and start transcription more often.

reasoningChain: Recall that transcription factors act on DNA, not directly on RNA polymerase in isolation.
Identify the specific region: the promoter, where RNA polymerase binds to start transcription.

inferredMistakes.text: Saying transcription factors bind "to DNA" in general without naming the promoter region specifically.
